question: The monster waves at Nazaré in Portugal get their extra size from a huge feature hidden on the seabed just offshore. What is it?
source_excerpt: Nazaré: The big-wave surfer's paradise born out of the largest underwater canyon in Europe

extra.why_interesting: Players assume giant waves come from giant storms or open ocean. The real reason is a hidden canyon on the seabed that concentrates the wave energy right in front of a small fishing town.
extra.verification_notes: Nazaré's giant waves are attributed to the Nazaré Canyon, a huge submarine canyon just offshore; a newer study only refines the mechanism, not the feature (https://livescience.com/planet-earth/rivers-oceans/nazare-the-big-wave-surfer-s-paradise-born-out-of-the-largest-underwater-canyon-in-europe).

explanation: The Nazaré Canyon is one of Europe's largest submarine canyons. It lets swells race in fast through deep water and then funnels and focuses them, so they rear up to record heights right beside the beach.

question: Mavericks, California's most feared big-wave spot, is named after one of the first to swim out there. Maverick wasn't a person, though. What was Maverick?
source_excerpt: named after a white German Shepherd named Maverick

extra.why_interesting: The name sounds like it honours a daring surfer or a rebel attitude. It actually comes from a dog that paddled out with its owner's group, which gives an unexpectedly sweet origin to one of the world's most feared waves.
extra.verification_notes: Mavericks is named after Maverick, a white German Shepherd that swam out with the first surfers, per Wikipedia and NBC; no newer developments contradict this.

explanation: Maverick was a white German Shepherd who swam out after his owner and friends. The wave that has since humbled the world's best surfers still carries the dog's name.
